chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
title: J. J. Johnson as the revolutionary modern trombonist
summary: Asked who did for trombone what Blanton did for bass, Jackson names J. J. Johnson, whom he first heard in Benny Carter's band at the Apollo.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: I'd like to ask you this. Like in bass, we always afforded Jimmy Blanton as having revolutionized bass playing.
As far as solos was concerned.
Well, who would you say was comparable to that in jazz trombone, that really just turned it around from what Big Green and Claude and --
I would say J. J. Johnson.
I call him the master right today whenever I see him.
He tells me I'm crazy but I still call him the master.
Well, how did that strike you when you first heard J. J. play?
I'd say -- Well, the first time I heard J. J., you know, was with Bennie Carter. That's the first time I heard J. J.
Uh-huh. Oh, he was in Bennie Carter's band?
Oh, God. It was in the forties, if I'm not mistaken. It was in the forties. Bennie Carter brought a band to the Apollo Theater.
And that's the first time I saw Al
Grey was with Bennie Carter, too.

But that's the first time I saw J. J. and then J. J. went with Basie. Of course he went to 52nd Street and he played with Basie too. And he was writing then, too, you know. J. J. was a very good arranger.
But J. J. to me was the first modern trombone player, to me, that had something before -- that changed the style of all trombone playing.
He fit into that era which to me was -- to me I would call it modern.
And nobody to me played like J. J. clear till this day if you listen to J. J.'s records or listen to J. J. play. To me, still, he's the greatest modern trombone player today, especially among us.
